meta_info.meta_description: Comparing the Godox AD100Pro and Godox V100: both deliver 100Ws, but serve very different needs. Learn the key differences and find which flash fits your shooting style.

content.h1: Godox AD100Pro vs Godox V100: Which 100Ws Flash Is Right for You?
content.intro: If you are shopping for a compact 100Ws flash from Godox, two models inevitably come up: the AD100Pro pocket strobe and the V100 round-head speedlight. On paper, both deliver 100 watt-seconds of power, support TTL and High-Speed Sync, work with the Godox X wireless system, and accept the AK-R1 magnetic accessory kit. Yet they are built for completely different workflows. The AD100Pro is a dedicated off-camera strobe designed to sit on a light stand, while the V100 is an on-camera speedlight that you mount directly onto your hotshoe. Choosing wrong means fighting your tool on every shoot. This comparison breaks down the real differences — power, controls, battery life, modifier compatibility, and real-world use cases — so you can pick the flash that actually fits how you shoot.

h2_sections.h2: 1. At a Glance: AD100Pro vs V100 Key Specs
h2_sections.content:
Before diving into hands-on impressions, here is a side-by-side look at what each flash brings on paper.

| Feature | Godox AD100Pro | Godox V100 |
|---------|---------------|------------|
| Maximum Power | 100 Ws | 100 Ws |
| Flash Type | Off-camera pocket strobe | On-camera round-head speedlight |
| Mounting | 1/4-inch thread (light stand / umbrella bracket) | Hotshoe (direct on-camera) |
| Dimensions | 120 × 76 × 76 mm (4.7 × 3.0 × 3.0 in) | 71.5 × 76 × 206 mm (2.8 × 3.0 × 8.1 in) |
| Weight (with battery) | 524 g (1.16 lb) | 619 g (1.36 lb) |
| Power Range | 1/1 – 1/256 (9 stops, 81 steps) | 1/1 – 1/256 (9 stops) |
| TTL | Yes (Canon, Nikon, Sony, Fujifilm, Olympus/Panasonic) | Yes (Canon, Nikon, Sony, Fujifilm, OM System) |
| HSS | Up to 1/8000s | Up to 1/8000s (1/80,000s with Sony global shutter) |
| Recycle Time (full power) | 0.01 – 1.5s | ~1.7s (0.8s with external PB960 pack) |
| Battery | 7.2V / 2600mAh Li-ion (removable) | 7.2V / 2980mAh Li-ion (removable, USB-C charging) |
| Full-Power Flashes per Charge | ~360 | ~400 (up to 70–100 consecutive) |
| LED Modeling Lamp | Built-in, 10 levels | 2W LED, 10 levels, 3300K ±200K |
| Wireless System | Godox 2.4G X (receiver) | Godox 2.4G X (master + receiver) |
| Wireless Groups | 5 | 5 |
| Display | OLED panel + physical buttons | 2.3-inch full-color touchscreen |
| Sub Flash | None | Detachable SU-1 fill flash |
| Auto Zoom | No (fixed coverage) | Yes (28–105 mm auto/manual) |
| External Power Pack | No | Yes (PB960 compatible) |
| Price (approx.) | $299 | $349 |

The numbers reveal the core split: the AD100Pro is a pure off-camera tool optimised for stand-mounted work with modifiers, while the V100 is a feature-loaded on-camera speedlight that can also go off-camera when needed.

Both the Godox AD100Pro and V100 share the same 100 Ws maximum output, so neither has a raw brightness advantage. The light quality, however, differs slightly due to head design.

The AD100Pro uses a bare-bulb-style design with a round magnetic head. It produces a natural, even spread with a colour temperature of 5800K ±200K — consistent and neutral, ideal for pairing with umbrellas, softboxes, and beauty dishes. Professional reviewers at SLR Lounge have noted that the AD100Pro delivers virtually no colour cast across power levels, which is critical for accurate skin tones.

The V100 uses a fresnel-based round head with auto zoom (28–105 mm). While slightly less bare than the AD100Pro in raw spread, the V100's light quality has been praised as excellent and neutral. The auto zoom function concentrates the beam at longer focal lengths, giving you more effective range when shooting at a distance — something the fixed-coverage AD100Pro cannot do. For on-camera use, this zoom ability is a genuine practical advantage.

In short: both produce professional-grade 100 Ws output. The AD100Pro favours bare, even spread for modifiers; the V100 gives you zoom flexibility for direct or bounced on-camera work.

h2_sections.h2: 3. Form Factor & Mounting: The Decisive Difference
h2_sections.content:
This is where these two flashes split into entirely different tools.

The AD100Pro is roughly the size and shape of a soda can (120 × 76 × 76 mm). It has no hotshoe foot — it mounts via a standard 1/4-inch thread on the bottom, meaning it goes on a light stand, an umbrella bracket, or a grip arm. There are two mounting slots (front and rear), so you can shift the balance point depending on whether you are using an umbrella or just hand-holding the bare flash. This off-camera-only design makes the AD100Pro the obvious choice when you are building a multi-light setup with stands, modifiers, and deliberate placement.

The V100 is a traditional speedlight form factor — 206 mm tall, with a hotshoe foot that slides directly onto your camera. It swivels 330° horizontally and tilts -7° to 120° vertically, giving you full bounce flexibility for event and wedding work. At 619 g with the battery, it is heavier than the AD100Pro on the scale, but it balances naturally on a camera body. The V100 can also go off-camera — just mount it on a stand with a cold shoe adapter — but its tall, front-heavy shape is less stable in modifiers than the AD100Pro's squat, low-profile body.

Bottom line: if you shoot on-camera at least some of the time, the V100 is the only choice of the two. If you exclusively shoot off-camera with modifiers, the AD100Pro is purpose-built for it.

The control experience on these two flashes could not be more different.

The AD100Pro uses a crisp OLED panel with physical buttons and a scroll wheel. It is functional, responsive, and works reliably even with gloves on. The menu is relatively simple — power, mode (TTL/M/Multi), group/channel, modelling light, and a few system settings. Experienced shooters will find it fast and distraction-free.

The V100 debuts Godox's first speedlight touchscreen — a 2.3-inch full-colour LCD with capacitive touch. Reviews from SLR Lounge and DIY Photography describe it as surprisingly responsive, closer to using a small smartphone than the clunky touch interfaces seen on older flashes. You can tap to switch between TTL and manual, swipe to adjust power, and one-tap pair with Godox X triggers. There is still a physical scroll wheel for those who prefer tactile control. The V100's new Chinese/English menu system is also significantly more intuitive than the old icon-based interface.

Which is better? The AD100Pro's button-and-dial interface is faster for muscle-memory operation in a studio. The V100's touchscreen is more beginner-friendly and faster for exploring settings on the fly.

Battery endurance and recycle speed are close, but the V100 pulls ahead in two specific areas.

The AD100Pro runs on a 7.2V / 2600mAh removable lithium-ion pack, rated for 360 full-power flashes. Recycle time is 0.01–1.5 seconds — lightning-fast at lower power and still solid at full output. The battery charges via a dedicated external charger, which means you cannot top it up via USB on the go.

The V100 uses a larger 7.2V / 2980mAh pack (the same VB30 battery as the V1 Pro), rated for approximately 400 full-power flashes. Full-power recycle is about 1.7 seconds — slightly slower than the AD100Pro — but the V100 can accept the Godox PB960 external power pack, which drops recycle time to roughly 0.8 seconds. Crucially, the V100 battery supports direct USB-C charging, so you can top up from a power bank or laptop between shoots.

Another V100 advantage: its advanced cooling system allows 70–100 consecutive full-power pops before thermal throttling kicks in. This is meaningful for wedding photographers who need to fire rapidly during fast-paced moments — the first dance, the bouquet toss, or outdoor portraits in rapid sequence. The AD100Pro has no stated burst rating, though its fanless passive design handles moderate studio use without issue.

Both flashes share the Godox round-head magnetic mount, so they work with the AK-R1 accessory kit (grid, snoot, gels, dome diffuser, wide-angle panel) and the AK-R21 projection attachment.

Where they diverge is larger modifiers. The AD100Pro mounts directly into the Godox S2 bracket, which adapts the flash to a Bowens mount — giving you access to hundreds of third-party softboxes, beauty dishes, snoots, and reflectors. This is a massive advantage for studio and location portrait work. The AD100Pro also has a built-in umbrella slot, so you can slide an umbrella shaft through the bracket without any additional adapter.

The V100 requires the S3 Speedlite Bracket (sold separately) for Bowens-mount modifiers. It works, but the setup is slightly more convoluted than the AD100Pro's native S2 integration. For on-camera use, the V100 is best paired with compact round-head modifiers — the AK-R22 collapsible diffusion dome, the tiny AK-R1 softbox, or bounce cards. The V100's detachable SU-1 sub flash also effectively acts as a built-in fill light when the main head is bounced off a ceiling, which is a unique creative tool the AD100Pro simply does not have.

Godox AD100Pro

| Pros | Cons |
|------|------|
| Compact, low-profile body (524 g) — ideal for stands and modifiers | No hotshoe mount — off-camera only |
| Faster full-power recycle (1.5s) | No auto zoom or beam concentration |
| Native Bowens mount via S2 bracket — huge modifier ecosystem | No touchscreen (buttons only) |
| Built-in umbrella slot — quick setup | Battery cannot charge via USB |
| 5 wireless groups, 32 channels | No sub flash or external power pack support |
| TIPA World Award winner for portable flash design | Lower full-power flashes per charge (360 vs 400) |

Godox V100

| Pros | Cons |
|------|------|
| Direct on-camera mounting — perfect for events and weddings | Heavier and taller — less stable on stands with large modifiers |
| 2.3-inch touchscreen — intuitive and fast | Slower full-power recycle (1.7s without external pack) |
| Auto zoom (28–105 mm) — better reach for distant subjects | Requires S3 bracket for Bowens modifiers (not native) |
| Detachable SU-1 sub flash for fill when bouncing | $50 more expensive than AD100Pro |
| USB-C direct battery charging — convenient on the go | No TIPA award pedigree for this form factor |
| 70–100 consecutive full-power flashes with active cooling | Fixed hotshoe foot — no 1/4-inch thread for direct stand mount |

Choose the Godox AD100Pro if:
- You shoot primarily off-camera — studio portraits, location fashion, product photography, or multi-light setups.
- You use large modifiers (softboxes, beauty dishes, parabolic umbrellas) and want native Bowens mount compatibility via the S2 bracket.
- You value the smallest possible form factor for travel — the AD100Pro is genuinely pocketable.
- You are building a multi-strobe kit and need consistent, low-profile heads that sit neatly on stands.
- Budget matters — at roughly $299, the AD100Pro is $50 cheaper.

Choose the Godox V100 if:
- You shoot on-camera at least some of the time — weddings, events, photojournalism, or run-and-gun portraiture.
- You want the flexibility of one flash that works both on-camera and off-camera (with a cold shoe adapter).
- You value a modern touchscreen interface and fast, intuitive control on the fly.
- You need rapid consecutive flashes — the 70–100 burst capability with active cooling is a real advantage for fast-paced work.
- You shoot with a Sony global shutter camera (A9 III) and want sync speeds up to 1/80,000s.
- USB-C battery charging matters for your workflow.

Ultimately, these two flashes are not really competitors — they are complementary tools. Many working photographers own both: the V100 on-camera for event coverage, and one or two AD100Pros on stands for the formal portrait segment of the same job. If you can only afford one, pick the form factor that matches how you actually shoot — not how you imagine you might shoot someday.

faq.question: Is Godox V100 more powerful than AD100Pro?
faq.answer: No, both the Godox V100 and AD100Pro deliver the same 100 Ws maximum power output. The difference lies in form factor and features, not raw brightness. The V100 adds auto zoom, a touchscreen, and a detachable sub flash, while the AD100Pro prioritises compact size and native modifier compatibility.

faq.question: Can you use the Godox AD100Pro on-camera?
faq.answer: No, the Godox AD100Pro does not have a hotshoe foot and cannot be mounted directly on a camera. It is a dedicated off-camera strobe designed to sit on a light stand, umbrella bracket, or grip arm via its 1/4-inch thread. For on-camera use, the V100 or V1 series is the correct choice.

faq.question: Does the Godox V100 overheat during long shoots?
faq.answer: The Godox V100 features an advanced cooling system that allows 70 to 100 consecutive full-power flashes before thermal throttling becomes a concern. In normal use where you are not firing at full power continuously, overheating is unlikely to be an issue. This is a significant improvement over earlier Godox speedlights.

faq.question: Which flash works better with softboxes: AD100Pro or V100?
faq.answer: The Godox AD100Pro works better with softboxes because its squat, low-profile body is more stable on a light stand and it mounts directly into the S2 bracket for native Bowens compatibility. The V100 can also be used with softboxes via the S3 bracket, but its tall speedlight shape is less balanced and the setup is more cumbersome.

faq.question: Can the Godox V100 and AD100Pro work together in the same wireless setup?
faq.answer: Yes. Both flashes use the Godox 2.4G Wireless X system with 5 groups and 32 channels. You can control both from the same XPro, X2T, or X3 trigger, mixing AD100Pros on stands with a V100 on-camera in a single coordinated lighting setup. This is a common workflow for wedding photographers.

FAQ

The V100 can also be used with softboxes via the S3 bracket, but its tall speedlight shape is less balanced.
